# Chart helpers

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-reference.swift from the Quiver 1.6.0 public API. Do not edit by hand. -->

Every API below exists in Quiver 1.0.0 and later unless it is tagged *(since X)*. Each entry is the declaration, then the first line of its documentation.

## Array extensions where Element: FloatingPoint

- `func rollingMean(window: Int) -> [Element]` — Calculates a rolling mean (moving average) over a specified window. Returns: Array of rolling means with the same length as the input
- `func exponentialMean(alpha: Element) -> [Element]` — Computes the exponential moving average, where recent values carry more weight. Returns: Array of smoothed values with the same length as the input *(since 1.0.1)*
- `func exponentialMean(span: Int) -> [Element]` — Computes the exponential moving average using a span-based smoothing factor. Returns: Array of smoothed values with the same length as the input *(since 1.0.1)*
- `func diff(lag: Int = 1) -> [Element]` — Calculates the difference between each element and the element a fixed number of periods before it. Returns: Array of differences with length equal to `count - lag`
- `func derivative(sampleRate: Element) -> [Element]` — Computes the numerical derivative by dividing consecutive differences by the sample rate (time between measurements). Returns: Array of rate-of-change values with length `count - 1` *(since 1.0.1)*
- `func percentChange(lag: Int = 1) -> [Element]` — Calculates the percentage change between each element and the element a fixed number of periods before it. Returns: Array of percentage changes with length equal to `count - lag`
- `func histogram(bins: Int) -> [(midpoint: Element, count: Int)] where Element : BinaryFloatingPoint` — Divides data into evenly spaced bins and counts the frequency of values in each. Returns: Array of tuples containing the midpoint and count for each bin
- `func histogram(rule: BinRule) -> [(midpoint: Element, count: Int)] where Element : BinaryFloatingPoint` — Divides data into evenly spaced bins using a named bin-selection rule. Returns: Array of tuples containing the midpoint and count for each bin. *(since 1.2.5)*
- `func quartiles() -> Quartiles<Element>? where Element : BinaryFloatingPoint, Element : Sendable` — Calculates the five-number summary and interquartile range of the data. Returns: A `Quartiles` value containing the five-number summary and IQR, or nil if the array is empty.
- `func percentile(_ p: Double) -> Element? where Element : BinaryFloatingPoint` — Calculates the value at a specific percentile using linear interpolation. Returns: The interpolated value at the given percentile, or nil if the array is empty or `p` is outside the valid range
- `func percentileRank(of value: Element) -> Element` — Calculates the percentile rank of a specific value within the array. Returns: The percentile rank between 0 and 100
- `func percentileRanks() -> [Element]` — Calculates the percentile rank for every value in the array. Returns: Array of percentile ranks (0-100) corresponding to each element
- `func scaled(to range: ClosedRange<Element>) -> [Element]` — Scales values to a target range using min-max normalization. Returns: Array of scaled values mapped to the target range
- `func asPercentages() -> [Element]` — Converts each value to its percentage of the total sum. Returns: Array where each value represents its percentage of the total sum
- `func standardized() -> [Element]` — Standardizes values using z-score normalization so the result has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Returns: Array of z-score standardized values, or empty array if standard deviation is zero
- `func groupBy(_ categories: [String], using method: AggregationMethod) -> [String : Element]` — Groups values by category labels and aggregates each group using the specified method. Returns: Dictionary mapping each category label to its aggregated value
- `func groupedData(by categories: [String], using method: AggregationMethod) -> [(category: String, value: Element)]` — Groups values by category and returns chart-ready tuples sorted by category name. Returns: Array of `(category, value)` tuples sorted alphabetically by category
- `func downsample(factor: Int, using method: AggregationMethod) -> [Element]` — Reduces the array size by grouping consecutive elements into fixed-size windows and aggregating each window into a single value. Returns: Array with length equal to `ceil(count / factor)`

## Array extensions where Element == [Double]

- `func stackedCumulative() -> [[Double]]` — Stacks multiple data series cumulatively so each series builds on the one below it. Returns: Array of arrays where each series is the cumulative sum of all preceding series
- `func stackedPercentage() -> [[Double]]` — Converts multiple data series into percentage-based stacking where each time point sums to 100%. Returns: Array of arrays where each value is the percentage contribution at that index
- `func correlationMatrix() -> [[Double]]` — Calculates the Pearson correlation matrix for multiple data series. Returns: A 2D array of Pearson correlation coefficients between all series pairs
- `func heatmapData(labels: [String]) -> [(x: String, y: String, value: Double)]` — Computes a correlation matrix and flattens it into labeled tuples for heatmap rendering. Returns: Array of `(x, y, value)` tuples suitable for heatmap visualization

## AggregationMethod

`enum AggregationMethod` — Specifies how values within a group or window are combined into a single result.

Conforms to: Equatable, Hashable.

- `case sum` — Sum all values in the group
- `case mean` — Calculate the arithmetic mean of the group
- `case count` — Count the number of values in the group
- `case min` — Select the minimum value in the group
- `case max` — Select the maximum value in the group
- `case percentage` — Sum all values per group, then normalize so all groups sum to 100 *(since 1.0.1)*

## BinRule

`enum BinRule` — Names a rule for choosing the number of bins in a histogram. *(since 1.2.5)*

Conforms to: Equatable, Hashable.

- `case squareRoot` — `k = ⌈√n⌉`. Depends only on sample size. Quick first look. *(since 1.2.5)*
- `case sturges` — `k = ⌈log₂(n) + 1⌉`. Sturges, 1926; assumes roughly normal data. *(since 1.2.5)*
- `case freedmanDiaconis` — `width = 2·IQR / n^(1/3)`, then `k = ⌈(max − min) / width⌉`. Freedman-Diaconis, 1981; robust to outliers. *(since 1.2.5)*
